newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: ASEAN sets proposals for nuclear arms-free zone.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN sets proposals for nuclear arms-free zone.

text.p: Southeast Asian nations on Friday agreed on new language for a treaty declaring the region a nuclear weapons-free zone in order to make it easier for nuclear powers to sign.

"We have agreed on certain proposals," Malaysian Foreign Ministry Secretary-General Abdul Kadir Mohamad said at the end of the two-day meeting of officials from the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).

The proposals, which he declined to disclose, offer new definitions of terms that would allow nuclear powers to sign a protocol to the treaty and still be guaranteed freedom of navigation and overflight in the region.
"We are going to go to them (the five nuclear powers) and say 'you say you have problems with the protocol. How about tackling the problem this way?'," Kadir said.

"We have different forms of wording...to take care of the legality problems," he said, after the first ASEAN senior officials meeting since Malaysia took over from Indonesia as chairman of the grouping.
The treaty bans signatory states from developing, manufacturing, acquiring, possessing or controlling nuclear weapons, although no constraints are applied to peaceful nuclear energy.
The ASEAN states -- Malaysia, Indonesia, Brunei, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam -- want the five declared nuclear powers to sign a protocol to the treaty.
Washington has objected to language which it says infringes on its ability to transit through the region under the "right of innocent passage" through territorial and archipelagic seas and straits.
Southeast Asia straddles key sea lanes linking the Indian Ocean with the South China Sea and the Pacific Ocean.
China's stand on the treaty is complicated by the fact that it has staked a claim to the whole of the South China Sea, diplomats said.
The treaty would be largely symbolic, the diplomats said. None of the countries in Southeast Asia has a nuclear weapons programme and none has the means to enforce the treaty.
But it is part of the group's long-standing ambition to resolve conflicts in Southeast Asia peacefully instead of pulling in major powers when crises erupt, they said.
